![Figure 3 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="cover-full.jpg"}

In *GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning* [[1]](#ref-1) ([ICLR 2026 Oral](https://iclr.cc/)), [Lakshya A. Agrawal](https://lakshyaaagrawal.github.io/) (UC Berkeley), [Matei Zaharia](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~matei/) (UC Berkeley / Databricks), [Omar Khattab](https://omarkhattab.com/) (MIT), and 14 co-authors across UC Berkeley, Stanford, Notre Dame, BespokeLabs.ai, Databricks, and MIT argue that natural-language reflection on sampled trajectories is a richer learning signal than scalar rewards, and introduce GEPA (Genetic-Pareto), a prompt optimizer that outperforms Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [[2]](#ref-2) while using far fewer rollouts.

> Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adapted to downstream tasks via reinforcement learning (RL) methods like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which often require thousands of rollouts to learn new tasks. We argue that the interpretable nature of language often provides a much richer learning medium for LLMs, compared to policy gradients derived from sparse, scalar rewards. To test this, we introduce *GEPA (Genetic-Pareto)*, a prompt optimizer that thoroughly incorporates *natural language reflection* to learn high-level rules from trial and error. Given any AI system containing one or more LLM prompts, GEPA samples trajectories (e.g., reasoning, tool calls, and tool outputs) and reflects on them in natural language to diagnose problems, propose and test prompt updates, and combine complementary lessons from the *Pareto frontier of its own attempts*. As a result of GEPA's design, it can often turn even just a few rollouts into a large quality gain. Across six tasks, *GEPA outperforms GRPO by 6% on average and by up to 20%, while using up to 35x fewer rollouts*. GEPA also *outperforms the leading prompt optimizer, MIPROv2, by over 10% (e.g., +12% accuracy on AIME-2025)*, and demonstrates promising results as an inference-time search strategy for code optimization. We release our code at <https://github.com/gepa-ai/gepa>.

## Method

A *compound AI system*, in the paper's (and [DSPy](https://dspy.ai/)'s) vocabulary, is a pipeline of one or more LLM-invoked *modules* — each a distinct prompted call (e.g., a first-hop query generator, a second-hop query generator, an answer generator in a multi-hop QA pipeline) — potentially interleaved with tool calls. Each module has its own prompt, which GEPA can optimize independently.

GEPA treats each prompt in a compound AI system as a *gene* and maintains a pool of candidate programs. At each iteration (Figure 3), GEPA proposes a new candidate using one of two *genetic operators* — a single-parent *mutation* or a two-parent *crossover* — and evaluates it on a minibatch. If the minibatch score improves over the parent, the candidate is promoted to evaluation on the full training set and added to the pool. The default operator is reflective mutation; crossover (Merge) fires opportunistically when the pool contains two candidates that share a common ancestor, have optimized disjoint sets of prompts, are both Pareto-optimal, and both beat the ancestor in aggregate — with a hard cap of five merges per run.

The two operators are:

- **Reflective Prompt Mutation** samples trajectories from one candidate — reasoning, tool calls, and tool outputs — and feeds them to a reflector LM that writes a natural-language diagnosis of what went wrong and proposes an edited prompt for a single module. Figure 5 traces this on PUPA [[3]](#ref-3) — a benchmark for *privacy-conscious delegation*, where a trusted local model must answer user queries containing personally identifiable information (PII) using an untrusted API model as a helper, without leaking PII. Starting from a short base instruction ("Create a privacy-preserving request for a powerful external LLM that can assist without learning private information about the user."), each successful child adds a concrete nuance the reflector extracted from a failure — expanded privacy strategies, explicit PII categories and generalizations, structured output and domain best-practices, then a detailed transformation rationale, ending at a strict exhaustive protocol that bans partial redaction and demands auditable zero-leakage. The prompt accumulates lessons rather than being rewritten wholesale. In the figure below, red arrows mark the promoted lineage from candidate 0 to the best candidate (11), with scores in parentheses.

![Figure 5 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure5.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="figure5-full.png"}

- **System-Aware Merge** takes two qualifying descendants of a common ancestor and assembles a child module-by-module. For each module, if one descendant changed the ancestor's prompt and the other left it untouched, the child inherits the changed version; if both descendants changed it, the child inherits from the higher-scoring parent (ties broken randomly); if neither changed it, it stays at the ancestor's version. No LLM call is made — the whole step is a textual combine over existing prompts, which is why the paper calls it *system-aware* crossover rather than a mutation. Merge works only when the two parents have explored disjoint modules, so complementary improvements can compose without stepping on each other.

Parent selection is Pareto-based rather than greedy. Instead of always mutating the best-scoring candidate, GEPA maintains a per-task score matrix over its history and samples parents from the [Pareto frontier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_front) — the set of candidates that no other candidate beats on every task — which prevents a locally strong candidate from dominating the search. The paper reports two named variants, "GEPA" using reflective mutation only and "GEPA+Merge" using both mutation and merge; both share the Pareto-based selector and the minibatch-then-full-set gate. The optimizer is agnostic to the downstream task: it needs a trajectory sampler, a metric, and a reflector LM.

## Results

Six tasks — HotpotQA [[4]](#ref-4), HoVer [[5]](#ref-5), IFBench [[6]](#ref-6), PUPA [[3]](#ref-3), AIME-2025 [[7]](#ref-7), and LiveBench-Math [[8]](#ref-8) — using [GPT-4.1 Mini](https://openai.com/index/gpt-4-1/) and [Qwen3-8B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-8B) as task models.

- **Qwen3-8B**: GEPA beats GRPO on five of the six benchmarks, losing only on AIME-2025. IFBench makes the gap sharp — GEPA reaches 38.61% after 678 rollouts, above GRPO's 35.88% at 24,000. Averaged across the six tasks, GEPA is +6% over GRPO and up to +20% on the best task, with up to $35\times$ fewer *rollouts* (trajectories sampled from the current policy during training). GEPA+Merge is less reliable here: it also trails GRPO on IFBench and PUPA, which the paper attributes to Merge's hyperparameters being tuned for GPT-4.1 Mini rather than Qwen3-8B.
- **GPT-4.1 Mini**: GEPA is evaluated as a drop-in prompt optimizer against MIPROv2 [[9]](#ref-9) in two settings (instruction-only "MIPROv2-No-Demos" and joint instruction-plus-few-shot "MIPROv2"), Trace [[10]](#ref-10) with its OptoPrime optimizer, and TextGrad [[11]](#ref-11) <!-- crosslink-todo: /posts/20260503-textgrad/ -->. GEPA wins on every benchmark, with margins as wide as 11% (HotpotQA, PUPA). The abstract highlights +12% on AIME-2025. A GEPA-Qwen-Opt variant optimized entirely on Qwen3-8B gets +9% when run on GPT-4.1 Mini without modification, outperforming every baseline that was optimized directly on GPT-4.1 Mini.

Beyond benchmarks, the paper reports GEPA as a promising inference-time search strategy for CUDA kernel optimization, iteratively improving kernels against a PyTorch-eager baseline.

![Tables 1 and 2 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1): benchmark results on Qwen3-8B (top) and GPT-4.1 Mini (bottom).](tables1-2.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="tables1-2-full.png"}

## My Notes

- **Reflection beats policy gradients**: GRPO wastes signal already present in each trajectory, in three ways.
  - *Information content*: GRPO consumes a trajectory as a single scalar reward (normalized against the group's own mean and standard deviation, the "Group Relative" that replaces PPO's learned critic), throwing away which tool call was wrong, which instruction was ambiguous, which demonstration misled the model. A reflector LM reading the same trajectory can name all three and edit the one prompt that caused the failure.
  - *Variance*: because each rollout contributes one noisy scalar, GRPO needs thousands of rollouts before the gradient estimate stabilizes. A natural-language critique encodes structured per-module diagnosis, so one rollout already yields usable signal.
  - *Credit assignment*: GRPO's policy-gradient update spreads the scalar reward across every token of every module in the rollout, even when only one module was responsible. Reflection attributes the failure to a single module and leaves the rest alone.
  - The same pattern shows up in [Self-Refine](/posts/20260516-self-refine/) and [Reflexion](/posts/20260516-reflexion/), where verbal feedback outperforms scalar reward at comparable compute. GEPA is the first paper I have seen that posts the head-to-head against GRPO on matched tasks.
- **The Pareto-frontier selector is the generalizable part**: Sampling mutation parents from the Pareto frontier rather than argmax prevents collapse to a single best candidate, which is the same mode-collapse problem that shows up in [evolutionary prompt search](/posts/20260515-promptbreeder/) and RL fine-tuning. The mechanism is general enough to drop into any iterative search where candidates have multi-dimensional scores (accuracy vs. cost, or task A vs. task B), and I expect to see it reused well past prompt optimization.
- **Beating MIPROv2 without Bayesian optimization**: This is a substantive methodological claim. MIPROv2 [[9]](#ref-9) <!-- crosslink-todo: /posts/20260503-miprov2/ --> spends its budget on a Bayesian surrogate over instruction and demonstration hyperparameters. GEPA discards the surrogate and spends the same budget on reflective rewrites plus merge. The result suggests the Bayesian model in MIPROv2 was under-using the trajectory information MIPROv2 already had access to, and the proposer was not reading the failures carefully enough. Several authors overlap between the two papers, so the comparison is a within-lab course-correction rather than an external critique.
- **The paper doesn't say what reflector it used**: Appendix E.2 lists Qwen3-8B and GPT-4.1 Mini as the *task* models but never specifies the reflection LM. The [gepa-ai/gepa repo](https://github.com/gepa-ai/gepa) quickstart pairs GPT-5 as reflector with GPT-4.1 Mini as task, a stronger model reading a weaker one's trajectories. Without the reflector spec or an ablation, we can't tell whether GEPA corroborates or contradicts the just-ask calibration [[12]](#ref-12) <!-- crosslink-todo: /posts/20260503-just-ask-calibration/ --> and [uncertainty-quantification](/posts/20260505-llm-uncertainty-survey/) findings that single-model self-evaluation is unreliable.
